author: Barry song
text:
The job titles on travel tech careers pages look nothing like they did two years ago.
"Principal Designer, AI Experiences."
"Senior Machine Learning Scientist — GenAI."
"AI Platform Engineer."
"Distinguished Scientist — Agentic AI."
These aren't hypothetical. They're live postings right now — across Booking.com, Skyscanner, Sabre, and Expedia.
Travel companies aren't just adopting AI tools. They're fundamentally rewriting what their engineering teams look like.
The data backs it up. Phocuswright reports 6 in 10 travel companies are now experimenting with or scaling agentic AI. McKinsey found half of organizations using AI expect to hire more data scientists within a year. Travel Tech Talent's 2026 industry analysis shows demand for ML engineers, MLOps specialists, and data platform architects outpacing supply by a widening margin.
Skyscanner reported a 23% productivity boost in engineering teams from generative AI adoption. Flight Centre's chief experience officer said AI competency is now central to how they recruit — not a nice-to-have, a baseline.
What's growing: AI infrastructure, data pipelines, model deployment, automation engineering.
What's quietly shrinking: generalist full-stack roles, UI-focused feature squads, traditional product management.
Here's the part that interests me as someone in recruitment.
The rush to build AI-native teams is real and necessary. But I keep seeing companies treat it as a swap — new AI talent in, domain veterans out — when it should be a merge.
Travel isn't like other tech sectors. The inventory is messy. Supplier relationships are built over years. Distribution networks have layers that no model can infer from a dataset. The people who understand why a rate plan nests inside an ancillary, or why the same hotel appears under three names across two feeds — that knowledge doesn't transfer in an onboarding doc.
The winners in travel tech over the next five years won't be the companies that hire the most AI scientists.
They'll be the ones that figure out how to pair deep industry expertise with AI capability — and keep both in the same room.
Hiring AI talent without retaining domain expertise isn't transformation. It's building a fast engine with no map.
What are you seeing in your industry? Is AI changing your team's composition, or just adding to it?

author: Mohit Rathod, open to work
text:
The distinction between a Data Scientist, an AI Engineer, and an NLP Specialist has widened dramatically. Yet, thousands of aspirants are still applying for all three using the exact same generic resume.  

This is the "Jack of All Trades" trap.  
When you claim to know a little bit of Excel, a bit of PyTorch, some SQL, and Transformer architectures on a single one-page resume, hiring teams don't see a versatile candidate—they see a beginner who hasn't mastered any part of the data lifecycle.  

The modern data ecosystem relies on specialized ownership:  

Infrastructure & Insights (Foundation): Data Engineers build the pipelines to ensure data is clean and reachable, while Data Analysts translate raw numbers into actionable business decisions.  

Predictions & Production (Intelligence): Data Scientists run statistical experiments and predictive modeling, while ML Engineers take those theoretical models and deploy them for millions of users.  

Specialized Frontiers (Perception & Systems): NLP Engineers work directly with Transformers (BERT, GPT), tokenization, and LLMs, while AI Engineers focus on end-to-end system integration and responsible AI practices.  

A generic resume is a rejected resume. Tailoring your projects, portfolio, and tool stack to one specific pillar is the highest-leverage move you can make for your career right now.  

For the hiring managers and senior leads in my network: Have you noticed a shift toward hiring hyper-specialists over generalists in your engineering teams lately, or do you still value broad-spectrum data roles in early-stage setups? Let's discuss in the comments.

author: Saikrishna Reddy, open to work
text:
🤖 I built an AI system that reviews my GitHub pull requests automatically. No button to click, no manual trigger, just push code and get real feedback in under 7 seconds.
Here's what's actually happening under the hood:
When I push a commit to a PR, a webhook fires to a Gateway service that verifies it's genuinely from GitHub (HMAC signature check). It gets parsed, deduped by commit SHA in Postgres, and queued on Redis. A Celery worker picks it up, fetches the real diff from GitHub's API, and runs it through a LangGraph pipeline where 4 specialized AI agents (Security, Static Analysis, Style, Architecture) review the code in parallel using GPT-4o-mini. Their findings get merged and deduplicated, then posted back as real inline comments through a registered GitHub App.
I built this while working full time as a Software Engineer at American Express on fraud detection and risk systems, and it's part of a deliberate push to build hands-on depth in agentic AI and multi-agent orchestration, the kind of systems companies like NVIDIA and Cisco are increasingly hiring for. Verified live across 3 separate repos so far.
Tech stack: LangGraph, FastAPI, Celery, Redis, PostgreSQL, Docker, GitHub App auth (JWT/RS256).
Video below shows the full flow, from a real git push to a real AI review appearing on the PR.

author: Pavan Sai Chandra, open to work
text:
I'm excited to share my new portfolio. 🤩 



When I sat down to build it, I realised I didn't want just another static page with a list of skills. I'm a Data Engineer. I spend my days designing systems that take raw, messy, high-volume data and turn it into something reliable that teams can actually trust. I wanted my portfolio to carry that same intention and craft. So I built it as an interactive 3D experience you can fly through.



A bit about what's inside:



🏦 A real-time banking data pipeline: PostgreSQL → Debezium → Kafka → S3 → Databricks, following the Medallion (Bronze/Silver/Gold) architecture, with CDC ingestion, SCD Type 2 modelling, and idempotent processing.



🚕 An Airflow-orchestrated ETL pipeline processing Uber ride-hailing data with PySpark, surfacing driver activity and peak-demand patterns.



▶️ A serverless AWS ETL pipeline using Glue, Lambda, and PySpark, landing analytics-ready data in S3.



🤖 A set of ML/DL projects from my MSc in AI: fraud detection on imbalanced data, stock trend prediction with sentiment analysis, CTR prediction with DeepFM, and cough detection from audio using CNNs.



This all sits on top of 4+ years of experience building AWS Lakehouse platforms, including pipelines ingesting from 20+ sources and processing 5+ TB of data every day, and my recently completed MSc in Artificial Intelligence at the University of Essex.



Building this reminded me why I love this field: there's real satisfaction in taking something complex and making it work cleanly, reliably, and at scale.
